screens.title: What is firewalld and how do zones work?
screens.narratorSegment: Firewalld is the dynamic firewall management solution on RHEL that replaces static iptables rules with a zone-based approach. A zone is a named security context that you assign to interfaces or sources to control what network traffic is allowed. Zones like public, internal, and trusted represent different trust levels. For example, you might place a network interface connected to your DMZ in the public zone with only HTTP and HTTPS allowed, while a management network interface is assigned to the internal or trusted zone with SSH enabled. The benefit is that you manage rules at the zone level rather than per-interface, which scales better across many hosts. A common misconception is that zones are only for physical interfaces; they also apply to sources and bridge interfaces. Another pitfall is assigning an interface to the wrong zone and unexpectedly opening or closing access. To verify your mapping, use firewall-cmd on the host and check the assigned interfaces and rules. Think about which interfaces in your inventory deserve stricter zones and why. In practical terms, define firewalld and the zone-based trust model used on rhel. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Ansible's ansible.posix.firewalld module
screens.narratorSegment: The ansible. posix. firewalld module is the primary Ansible interface to manage firewalld. Its main parameters include zone, service, port, rich_rule, state, permanent, and immediate. Use zone to target the security context, service to open named services like http or ssh, and port to open a specific TCP or UDP port with the 'port' parameter format such as 8080/tcp. The state parameter toggles whether the rule is enabled or disabled. screens.title: Runtime vs Permanent configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Firewalld exposes two configuration layers: runtime and permanent. Runtime changes affect the active firewall immediately but are lost when firewalld restarts or the system reboots. Permanent changes are written to disk and survive reboots but require a reload to affect runtime unless immediate application is used. Ansible exposes both behaviors via the permanent and immediate parameters. For production you typically set permanent: yes to ensure persistence and immediate: yes so the change takes effect now. A common mistake is to set only immediate: yes and assume persistence — that leads to rules disappearing after a reboot. Conversely, setting only permanent: yes without immediate: yes delays the rule until a reload. Use both flags to avoid that gap. Always validate by rebooting a test host or restarting firewalld to confirm the permanent rules are applied as expected. Consider documenting whether your playbooks rely on immediate application or scheduled reloads. Runtime vs Permanent configuration means use permanent for persistence and immediate to apply to runtime; set both for immediate and lasting changes.. In practical terms, understand the difference and how to apply both with ansible. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.narratorSegment: Rich rules give you granular control beyond service and port-based rules. They allow you to match on source addresses, protocols, ports, and choose an action like accept, reject, or drop. In Ansible the rich_rule parameter accepts a rich rule string that mirrors firewalld syntax, for example a rule that allows SSH only from a specific IP address. Remember to set both permanent: yes and immediate: yes for these rules as well. After applying a rich rule, validate with firewall-cmd --list-all --zone=public and test connectivity from the allowed and disallowed source addresses to confirm behavior. Rich rules for granular control means rich rules provide the granularity to restrict access by source, protocol, and action when needed for least-privilege controls.. Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Playbook sequence
configure_firewall.yml (template)
---
- name: Configure Firewalld
  hosts: webservers
  become: yes

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure firewalld service is running and enabled
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: firewalld
        state: started
        enabled: yes

    - name: Allow TCP port 8080 in public zone
      ansible.posix.firewalld:
        zone: public
        port: 8080/tcp
        state: enabled
        permanent: yes
        immediate: yes

    - name: Allow ICMP (ping) from any source in public zone using a rich rule
      ansible.posix.firewalld:
        zone: public
        rich_rule: 'rule protocol value="icmp" accept'
        state: enabled
        permanent: yes
        immediate: yes

    - name: Remove HTTP service from public zone (if present)
      ansible.posix.firewalld:
        zone: public
        service: http
        state: disabled
        permanent: yes
        immediate: yes
Action checklist
  • Run playbook in check mode to preview.
  • Ensure SSH isn't removed before other rules are in place.
  • Verify with firewall-cmd and remote tests after apply.
Why it matters
Following a safe sequence prevents accidental lockout and ensures rules persist across reboots.

In this module you will learn how to use Ansible to manage firewalld on Red Hat Enterprise Linux systems. We start by understanding firewalld's zone-based model and why zones make it easier to apply consistent policies across interfaces. Then we'll use the ansible. posix. firewalld module to open services and ports, set rules to be both immediate and permanent, and write rich rules for granular access control. You will see concrete playbook examples for common tasks like enabling HTTP and HTTPS, opening a custom port, and creating a rich rule to restrict SSH to a single management IP. We'll also cover common mistakes, such as forgetting permanent changes or accidentally blocking SSH, and practical safeguards like allowing SSH early and using check mode. By the end of this lesson you'll be prepared to write safe, repeatable firewall playbooks that maintain a consistent security posture across your infrastructure. Consider how automation reduces human error and ask yourself which hosts in your inventory need tighter zone assignments.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain firewalld's zone-based model and why zones help manage trust between networks. You will use the ansible. posix. firewalld module to add and remove services and ports, and to apply rules immediately and persistently. You will write and apply rich rules to permit or restrict traffic based on source addresses or protocols. Finally, you will adopt safety practices such as ensuring SSH access, testing changes with check mode, and verifying rules with firewall-cmd. Each objective combines a practical skill and its operational rationale so you understand not just how to run a task, but why it is important for reliable security. For example, knowing the difference between runtime and permanent configurations prevents accidental loss of rules after a reboot. These skills are central to maintaining consistent firewall posture across many servers without introducing outages.

This second objectives slide focuses on safe practice and validation. You will learn to run playbooks in check mode to preview changes and to use firewall-cmd on a target host to confirm active rules. You will practice writing a playbook that enables firewalld, opens a custom TCP port, adds a rich rule for ICMP, and removes an existing service. You will also adopt the habit of adding an explicit SSH allow for your control node's IP as one of the first rules to prevent accidental lockout. These practices are essential in real environments where remote access is critical. For example, when you open a new application port, testing with check mode and verifying with firewall-cmd prevents interruptions. This slide emphasizes that automation should be reversible, previewable, and tested before production rollout.

Firewalld is the dynamic firewall management solution on RHEL that replaces static iptables rules with a zone-based approach. A zone is a named security context that you assign to interfaces or sources to control what network traffic is allowed. Zones like public, internal, and trusted represent different trust levels. For example, you might place a network interface connected to your DMZ in the public zone with only HTTP and HTTPS allowed, while a management network interface is assigned to the internal or trusted zone with SSH enabled. The benefit is that you manage rules at the zone level rather than per-interface, which scales better across many hosts. A common misconception is that zones are only for physical interfaces; they also apply to sources and bridge interfaces. Another pitfall is assigning an interface to the wrong zone and unexpectedly opening or closing access. To verify your mapping, use firewall-cmd on the host and check the assigned interfaces and rules. Think about which interfaces in your inventory deserve stricter zones and why. The ansible. posix. firewalld module is the primary Ansible interface to manage firewalld. Its main parameters include zone, service, port, rich_rule, state, permanent, and immediate. Use zone to target the security context, service to open named services like http or ssh, and port to open a specific TCP or UDP port with the 'port' parameter format such as 8080/tcp. The state parameter toggles whether the rule is enabled or disabled. Two parameters are critical for operational behavior: permanent controls whether the change is written to persistent configuration, and immediate controls if the change is applied to the runtime configuration now. A common operational pattern is to set both permanent: yes and immediate: yes so the rule is active immediately and survives reboots. Firewalld exposes two configuration layers: runtime and permanent. Runtime changes affect the active firewall immediately but are lost when firewalld restarts or the system reboots.
